channel.title: Multilingual on Best of AI
channel.description: Recent content in Multilingual on Best of AI

item.title: Memrise
item.description:
Memrise built its approach on memory science. Learners review words and phrases at spaced intervals, so the items they find hardest come back more often. Short videos of real people speaking in everyday situations expose learners to natural accents and pace, which differs from the robotic audio common in older courses.

Newer features add conversation. AI chat partners let users practice dialogues, ask for corrections, and role play situations like ordering food or booking a room. The app offers many languages, with courses created by the company and, in earlier years, by community members, plus a mobile experience designed for short daily sessions.

item.title: Speak
item.description:
Speak puts spoken practice first. Instead of tapping through vocabulary drills, you speak aloud in lessons that simulate real situations such as ordering food, introducing yourself, or having a job interview. The app listens, corrects pronunciation and grammar, and prompts you to try again, so you gain confidence speaking, which many apps neglect.

An AI tutor handles open-ended conversation. You can discuss topics you choose, practice roleplays, and ask the tutor to explain mistakes, with the system adapting to your level. The app began with a focus on English for Korean speakers and has expanded to teach other languages, with courses designed for particular native languages. It was developed with backing from OpenAI’s startup fund.

item.title: Trados Studio
item.description:
Trados is one of the best-known tools among professional translators. When translators work on a document, Trados breaks it into segments and checks a translation memory for matches from previous projects, offering exact and fuzzy matches so work is reused and terminology stays consistent. That improves speed and quality, especially on repetitive technical content, and lowers costs for clients who pay by new words.

The product has evolved with the technology. It integrates machine translation engines, including adaptive and neural options, and supports AI-assisted features for suggestions and quality checks. Trados Enterprise is a cloud version for teams and organizations, supporting collaboration, project management, and workflows with vendors, while the desktop Studio remains popular among freelancers and agencies.

item.title: Qwen-Image-3.0
item.description: Alibaba announced Qwen-Image-3.0 on July 21, 2026 with invite-only access, then opened it fully on August 5. The third generation of Alibaba’s image line, it is built around accepting much longer instructions than its predecessor, up to roughly 4,500 tokens versus about 1,000 for Qwen-Image 2.0, so it can compose dense, information-heavy layouts like infographics, slide decks, and UI mockups in a single pass. It also renders small text accurately down to about 10 pixels across a dozen languages, an area where earlier image models tended to produce garbled or illegible characters.

item.title: Aquila
item.description: Aquila is the Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence’s first open bilingual language model, released in 2023 as a 7-billion-parameter base model trained on Chinese and English text. BAAI built it on a GPT-style architecture with a custom tokenizer designed to handle Chinese text more efficiently than tokenizers borrowed from English-first models, and it supports a 2,048-token context window. The release included both a base pretrained model and an AquilaChat instruction-tuned variant, along with a code-focused AquilaCode model.

item.title: Aquila2
item.description:
Aquila2 is the Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence’s second-generation bilingual model family, released in October 2023 as a follow-up to the original Aquila. The family spans 7B and 34B base models, chat-tuned AquilaChat2 variants, and long-context versions extended to 16,000 tokens through positional-encoding interpolation, plus experimental 70B checkpoints. BAAI reported that Aquila2-34B outperformed other open Chinese-English models of similar size on Chinese-language benchmarks at the time of release.

The models are released under the Apache 2.0 license for the codebase, with model weights governed by BAAI’s own Aquila license agreement that allows commercial use under certain conditions. Aquila2 targeted developers who needed strong bilingual performance without relying on a Western base model like LLaMA, and it remained one of BAAI’s main open releases until the organization shifted more attention toward its FlagEmbedding and other specialized model lines.

item.title: Aya 23
item.description: Aya 23 is a family of multilingual language models that Cohere For AI, Cohere’s research lab, released in May 2024, covering 23 languages including Arabic, Chinese, Hindi, Japanese, Russian, and Spanish alongside English. It shipped in two sizes, 8B and 35B parameters, both built on Cohere’s Command architecture and initialized from a pretrained checkpoint before further multilingual training. The 35B version is the one tracked here, with an 8192-token context window aimed at retrieval and instruction-following tasks across languages that are usually underserved by English-centric open models. Cohere released the weights under a CC-BY-NC 4.0 license with an acceptable-use addendum, so it’s free for research and non-commercial use but requires a separate commercial agreement for production deployment. It followed the original Aya project, which had focused on data and evaluation for 101 languages, by narrowing scope to a smaller set of languages in exchange for stronger per-language quality.

item.title: BGE-M3
item.description: BGE-M3 is a text embedding model from BAAI, described in a paper published in February 2024, and the name refers to three things it does at once: multi-linguality across more than 100 languages, multi-granularity handling of inputs up to 8192 tokens, and multi-functionality in that it produces dense vectors, sparse lexical weights, and ColBERT-style token vectors from a single forward pass. It has 568 million parameters, which is modest next to large LLMs but is trained specifically for retrieval rather than generation. That combination let it post state-of-the-art results at the time on the multilingual MIRACL benchmark and the cross-lingual MKQA benchmark, since a single model could substitute for what previously required separate dense and sparse retrieval systems. BAAI released it under the MIT license on Hugging Face, and it’s widely used in retrieval-augmented generation pipelines that need to search across documents in multiple languages or documents longer than the 512-token limit typical of earlier BERT-based embedding models.

item.title: BLOOM
item.description: BLOOM is a 176 billion parameter language model built by BigScience, a year-long collaboration of over a thousand researchers coordinated through Hugging Face with compute donated by the French government’s Jean Zay supercomputer. It launched in July 2022 as an answer to closed models like GPT-3, trained on the ROOTS corpus covering 46 natural languages and 13 programming languages, with a deliberate emphasis on underrepresented languages that most large labs ignored at the time. The project published its training data, code, and a full technical report alongside the weights, which was rare for a model at that scale.

item.title: BLOOMZ
item.description: BLOOMZ is BigScience’s instruction-tuned version of BLOOM, released in late 2022 by fine-tuning the base 176 billion parameter model on xP3, a large collection of multilingual tasks phrased as natural-language instructions. The point of the project was cross-lingual generalization: BLOOMZ was tuned mostly on English instructions but showed it could follow instructions in languages it had never seen paired with instructions during fine-tuning, as long as it had encountered that language during BLOOM’s original pretraining. That made it one of the earlier public demonstrations that instruction-following skills transfer across languages rather than needing separate tuning for each one.

item.title: Canary
item.description: Canary is a family of speech models from NVIDIA’s NeMo team, with the flagship Canary-1B released in April 2024. Unlike a typical ASR model that only transcribes audio, Canary handles both speech recognition and speech translation across English, French, German, and Spanish, converting spoken audio into text in the same language or translating it into another. It combines a FastConformer encoder with a transformer decoder, an architecture NVIDIA tuned to get strong accuracy from a comparatively small model, and it topped the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard against competitors several times its size when it launched.

item.title: Cohere Embed Multilingual v3
item.description: Cohere Embed Multilingual v3 is a text embedding model Cohere released in November 2023 for search, retrieval-augmented generation, and semantic similarity tasks across more than 100 languages. It takes input text up to 512 tokens and outputs a 1024-dimension vector by default, with support for shorter 384 or 768 dimension embeddings when a team wants faster search or lower storage cost. Cohere trained it alongside an English-only sibling, Embed English v3, and pitched both as an upgrade over v2 because they weight passages by how relevant they are likely to be, not just how similar they are, which cuts down on noisy retrieval results in RAG pipelines. It’s priced at $0.10 per million tokens through the Cohere API and is also distributed through AWS, Azure, and Oracle Cloud marketplaces. Cohere has since released newer Embed v4 models, and some cloud providers such as Oracle now list v3 as a legacy or deprecated option, though it remains available through Cohere’s own API and Hugging Face.

item.title: jina-embeddings-v3
item.description: jina-embeddings-v3 is Jina AI’s multilingual text embedding model, released in September 2024. It has 570 million parameters and supports 89 languages, with a context window of 8,192 tokens using rotary position embeddings. The model uses task-specific LoRA adapters for different use cases such as query-document retrieval, clustering, classification, and text matching, so a single set of weights can be adapted to different jobs without full retraining. It also supports Matryoshka representation learning, which lets users truncate the output embedding down from its default 1024 dimensions to as low as 32 while keeping most of the retrieval quality. On the MTEB benchmark, Jina AI reported that v3 outperformed proprietary embeddings from OpenAI and Cohere on English tasks and beat multilingual-e5-large-instruct across multilingual tasks. It is released under a CC BY-NC 4.0 license, which permits free use for research and evaluation but requires a commercial license for production use at scale.

item.title: memoQ
item.description:
memoQ helps translators work faster and stay consistent. As a translator works through a document, the tool shows matches from a translation memory of earlier work and terms from a glossary, so repeated phrases are translated the same way. Machine translation can provide suggestions that the translator edits.

For teams, memoQ’s server and cloud products manage projects, assign work to translators and reviewers, and track deadlines and costs. It supports many file formats and quality checks, and integrates with machine translation engines and AI services, including large language models for suggestions and review.

item.title: Smartling
item.description:
Smartling connects content systems to translators. Websites, apps, and documents flow in through integrations, and Smartling applies translation memory and machine translation, then routes text to human linguists where quality matters most. Translations return to the source system.

Features include visual context for translators, glossaries, quality scoring, and AI that translates and edits at scale. The company has pushed AI-first workflows to reduce cost and time, and reports on translation quality and spend.

item.title: SYSTRAN
item.description:
SYSTRAN is among the oldest names in machine translation. Its modern products use neural models, offered as an API, a desktop app, and server software that can run inside an organization’s own network. This matters for sensitive documents.

Customization lets organizations tune translation to their terminology, and the platform handles many file formats and language pairs. Government and corporate customers use it for large volumes of content.

SYSTRAN is sold by subscription and license. General-purpose language models now compete in translation quality. Alternatives include DeepL, Google Cloud Translation, Microsoft Translator, Amazon Translate, and Lilt. SYSTRAN suits organizations needing private, deployable translation.

item.title: Babbel
item.description: Babbel focuses on getting learners to speak useful phrases quickly. Lessons last around ten to fifteen minutes and follow real-life topics such as ordering food, travel, work, and introductions. Content is written by teams of linguists and teachers, and each course is designed for a speaker of a specific native language, so explanations address the mistakes people with that background typically make. It covers more than a dozen languages, including Spanish, French, German, Italian, and Portuguese.

item.title: Busuu
item.description:
Busuu offers courses in several popular languages, organized by the levels of the Common European Framework, from beginner to upper-intermediate. Lessons teach vocabulary, grammar, listening, reading, and speaking in short sessions, and a review system revisits words to help you remember them. Learners can set a goal, such as being ready for travel or a certain level, and the study plan adjusts to fit.

The feature that sets it apart is community feedback. You can write or record a short answer and have it corrected by native speakers who use the app, which gives real human feedback on your output. AI tools add conversation practice, personalized review, and explanations of mistakes. Some plans offer certificates and exam preparation for recognized language tests.

item.title: DeepL
item.description:
DeepL built its reputation on translations that read more naturally than many competitors, especially for European languages. You paste text or upload a document, such as a Word file, PDF, or PowerPoint, and get a translation that keeps the formatting. Options let you choose formal or informal tone, add glossaries for specific terms, and see alternative wordings for phrases.

The product has expanded into a broader language platform. DeepL Write improves and rephrases text in the same language, DeepL Voice translates live conversations and meetings, and browser extensions and desktop apps translate as you work. An API serves developers and enterprises, and newer agent features automate tasks. Business plans add data security, which promises that texts are not used for training, plus team glossaries.

item.title: Duolingo
item.description:
Duolingo made language learning feel like a game. Lessons take a few minutes and mix translation, matching, listening, and speaking exercises. Streaks, experience points, and leagues reward consistency, and the friendly design and persistent reminders turned it into one of the most used education apps in the world. Courses cover languages from Spanish and French to Japanese, Korean, and smaller options, and it also offers math, music, and chess.

AI is a growing part of the product. A paid tier called Max includes features such as explanations of why an answer was right or wrong and role-play conversations with an AI character, and video call practice lets learners speak with an animated character. The company also uses AI to generate and personalize lesson content, which has been controversial among some users and staff who worry about quality and jobs.

item.title: Google Translate
item.description: Google Translate is the translation tool most people try first. You type or paste text and get a translation in a second, with the language detected automatically. The mobile app adds the features travelers rely on: a camera mode that replaces text on signs and menus, a conversation mode that translates both sides of a spoken exchange, handwriting input, and offline language packs that work without a connection. Chrome can translate whole web pages, and you can upload documents and get a translated copy.

item.title: Happy Scribe
item.description:
Happy Scribe converts speech into text. You upload an audio or video file, or connect a source like Zoom or YouTube, and receive a transcript in minutes with speaker labels and timestamps. It supports many languages and dialects, which suits journalists, researchers, podcasters, and companies that work in several markets. A browser editor lets you listen while you correct the text.

Subtitling is a major use. The service can generate subtitles and captions for videos, translate them into other languages, and export in standard formats for YouTube, Vimeo, and video editors. For cases where accuracy matters more, such as legal or broadcast work, you can order human-made transcripts and subtitles, which cost more and take longer. An API and integrations connect it to workflows.

item.title: Lokalise AI
item.description:
Lokalise helps teams ship products in multiple languages. Developers and designers connect their code repositories and design files, and Lokalise collects the text that needs translating, lets translators and reviewers work on it in an editor with context, and sends finished translations back. Integrations with GitHub, GitLab, Figma, and content systems keep localization in step with development rather than delaying releases.

AI sits at the center of recent versions. It can translate new strings with models that take glossaries, tone, and context into account, flag likely errors, and score translation quality so humans focus on the content that needs attention. Translation memory reuses approved translations for consistency and cost savings, and workflows route content to in-house teams or translation vendors. Reporting shows progress by language.

item.title: Microsoft Translator
item.description:
Microsoft Translator covers the common translation needs. You can type or paste text, speak into a phone for conversation translation, translate images and documents, and use offline language packs when traveling. Multi-device conversation mode lets several people speak in different languages and see translations on their own screens, which suits meetings and travel.

It’s integrated throughout Microsoft products. Teams offers live captions and translated meetings, Office apps can translate documents and text, and Edge translates web pages. For developers and businesses, Azure AI Translator provides APIs for text, document, and speech translation, with custom models and glossaries, and options to run in containers.

item.title: Otter.ai
item.description:
Otter.ai joins online meetings, transcribes the conversation as it happens, and produces notes people can search and share. Speakers are labeled, key points are summarized, and action items are pulled out, so attendees can focus on the discussion instead of taking notes.

Features include an assistant that can answer questions about a meeting or across past meetings, automatic sharing of notes with attendees, and integrations with calendars and collaboration tools. Mobile and web apps handle in-person conversations, lectures, and interviews.

item.title: Phrase
item.description:
Phrase helps companies translate software and content into many languages. Developers connect repositories and design tools, and new text is sent to translators or machine translation, then returned to the product when approved. Translation memory reuses earlier work and glossaries keep terminology consistent.

The platform brings together several products that grew from a merger: a translation management system, a string management tool for software teams, and a computer-assisted translation editor. AI translation engines and quality estimation reduce the amount of human review needed for lower-risk content.

item.title: Rev
item.description:
Rev started as a human transcription marketplace and added automatic transcription as speech recognition improved. Users upload audio or video, and receive a transcript within minutes from the AI service, or within hours from human transcribers who deliver higher accuracy. The choice lets you trade cost and speed for precision, which matters for legal proceedings, journalism, and broadcast captions.

Beyond transcripts, Rev offers captions and subtitles in many languages, translation, and a web editor for correcting and exporting text. Meeting tools record calls and produce notes, and an API supports developers who want to add transcription to products. Accessibility compliance is a big use, because captions help meet legal requirements for education and media.

item.title: Reverso
item.description:
Reverso is known for context. Beyond a plain translation, it shows examples of the word or phrase used in real texts, such as books, subtitles, and documents, with the original and translation side by side. That helps learners and translators choose the right expression, understand nuance, and see how phrases are typically used in each language.

The product includes several tools. A translator handles text and documents, Reverso Context is the example search, and a grammar and spell checker works across languages. Verb conjugators, vocabulary lists, and flashcards support learning, and AI features paraphrase and improve text. Browser extensions and mobile apps make it available while reading or writing.

item.title: Rosetta Stone
item.description: Rosetta Stone teaches by immersion. Instead of translating from your own language, lessons pair images with words and phrases in the target language, so you learn by association, the way children pick up a first language. Lessons build from simple vocabulary to conversation, with exercises on listening, reading, writing, and speaking. It has been a recognized name in language learning for decades and sells courses in about two dozen languages.

item.title: Smartcat
item.description:
Smartcat brings machine and human translation together. A company uploads documents or connects content sources, receives AI translation immediately, and can request human review from freelance linguists or agencies in its marketplace, all with translation memory and glossaries.

Workflow tools manage projects, deadlines, and payments, and the platform supports many file types and integrations. AI agents handle tasks such as quality checks, and the pricing model aims to keep costs lower than traditional agencies.

item.title: SubtitleBee
item.description:
SubtitleBee automates subtitles. You upload a video, choose the spoken language, and the tool transcribes it and creates timed captions, which you can edit in a simple editor. It supports many languages and can translate subtitles into others, helping creators reach international audiences. Typical users are YouTubers, social media managers, educators, and marketers, who need captions because many viewers watch with the sound off.

Style options let captions fit a brand: you can change fonts, colors, positions, and highlight words as they are spoken, which is a popular look on short-form video. Subtitles can be exported as files for use in other editors or burned into the video itself. Plans are tied to the amount of video processed, and the product is in a crowded category.

item.title: Pimsleur
item.description:
Pimsleur is an audio-first method developed by linguist Paul Pimsleur. Each short lesson has the learner listen to a conversation, repeat phrases aloud, and answer prompts, with vocabulary reintroduced at expanding intervals so it moves into memory. Lessons are designed for use while commuting or doing chores.

The app offers many languages and adds features such as reading lessons, flashcards, and speech practice. Its approach centers on speaking and listening more than grammar rules or writing.

item.title: Preply
item.description:
Preply matches students with tutors. Learners browse profiles, filter by language, price, and availability, book a trial lesson, and then continue with a tutor of their choice. Lessons take place on the platform’s video classroom with tools for sharing materials.

The company has added AI to support learning between lessons. Speaking practice partners simulate conversation, summaries and homework are generated from lessons, and vocabulary tools help with review. Tutors can use AI to prepare materials.

item.title: Submagic
item.description:
Submagic speeds up editing of talking-head clips. A creator uploads a video, the tool transcribes speech, adds styled captions that highlight words as they are spoken, and suggests emojis, sound effects, and B-roll to keep viewers engaged.

Templates provide the caption looks seen on popular social videos, and users can edit text, timing, and style. Tools for trimming silence and magic clips from longer videos add to the toolkit. Multiple languages are supported.
